section_summary: This section continues a detailed inventory of Japanese diplomatic property in Chile, then surveys the transfer, custody, inspection, microfilming, storage, sale, and funding of Japanese diplomatic and consular archives around the world after Japan's surrender. Reports from missions in Latin America, Europe, the Middle East, and the Pacific describe differing local arrangements involving Allied representatives, protecting powers, and territorial governments. The section ends with a long Lima despatch documenting Peru's transfer procedures, cash deposits, furniture storage, receipts, and inventories.

subfiles.title: Continuation of inventory of Japanese diplomatic property in Santiago
subfiles.from: Japanese and Swedish custodial representatives in Santiago
subfiles.about: Continues the itemized inventory of Japanese diplomatic property held in Santiago.
subfiles.summary: The continuation lists appliances, curtains, pictures, screens, works of art, tableware, books, papers, records, cooking equipment, official seals, flags, and documents by box number. A concluding note records damaged, missing, sold, or separately stored objects, including items at the Swedish Legation.

subfiles.title: Inventory of the Japanese Military Attaché's Office
subfiles.from: Kiyoshi Yamagata, Folke Wennerberg, and Curt Hartzell
subfiles.to: Property-transfer record; enclosed with Despatch No. 13,047
subfiles.about: Lists the contents of fifteen boxes belonging to the Japanese Military Attaché's Office in Chile.
subfiles.summary: The boxes contained tableware, office supplies, books, papers, appliances, furniture, a typewriter, radio, refrigerator, carpet, cupboard, and steel case. The signatories certified that the property had been counted, handed over, and received in Santiago.

subfiles.title: List of principal articles in Japanese Legation Special Box No. 7
subfiles.about: Identifies the principal documentary contents of a special box surrendered by the Swedish Chargé d'Affaires.
subfiles.summary: The box held official correspondence, accounts, inventory and general reports, passport forms, trade and naval studies, industrial notes, Yamagata's diaries, personal papers, and shipping-company records. The list was prepared after delivery of the box to the U.S. Ambassador on behalf of the Allied Powers.

subfiles.title: Swedish note concerning surrender of Japanese property in Chile
subfiles.from: Folke Wennerberg, Swedish Legation in Santiago
subfiles.to: Joaquín Fernández y Fernández, Chilean Minister of Foreign Affairs
subfiles.about: Notifies Chile that Japanese diplomatic and consular property will be delivered to an Allied representative.
subfiles.summary: The note states that the Japanese minister in Stockholm, acting on instructions from Tokyo, requested delivery of Japanese diplomatic and consular property formerly entrusted to the Swedish representative. It also asks permission for the Swedish Legation to continue routine protection of Japanese citizens in Chile.

subfiles.title: Departmental distribution memorandum for Santiago Despatch No. 13,047
subfiles.to: Military Intelligence Division; Office of Naval Intelligence; Federal Bureau of Investigation; Office of Strategic Services
subfiles.about: Circulates the Santiago report on the delivery of Japanese official property and archives.
subfiles.summary: The Department forwarded a copy of Despatch No. 13,047 to intelligence and investigative agencies. The enclosure concerned delivery by the Swedish minister to the American ambassador as representative of the Allied Powers.

subfiles.title: Circular requesting reports on Japanese records and property
subfiles.to: American diplomatic missions, with listed exceptions
subfiles.about: Requests mail reports on the procedures used to take over Japanese diplomatic and consular archives and property.
subfiles.summary: Missions were directed to describe the records and property obtained and the procedures followed. The Department advised them to follow, where practicable, earlier instructions governing German archives and property.

subfiles.title: Circular on Japanese instructions implementing MacArthur's directive
subfiles.to: American diplomatic missions, with listed exceptions
subfiles.about: Reports that Japan had instructed its overseas missions to comply with General MacArthur's directive.
subfiles.summary: The Department stated that Tokyo sent telegraphic instructions on October 31. Reports from Stockholm and Bern indicated that Japanese representatives had received or acted upon those instructions on November 1.

subfiles.title: Rio de Janeiro telegram on examination and microfilming of Japanese archives
subfiles.about: Reports the joint Allied inspection and microfilming of archives at the former Japanese Embassy in Rio.
subfiles.summary: American, British, Chinese, Brazilian, military, naval, and legal representatives examined archives at Rua das Laranjeiras 192 while microfilming began on site. The embassy also reported furniture, cash, and property or records at São Paulo, Santos, and Belém, and requested instructions for their disposition.

subfiles.title: Panama telegram requesting action on deteriorating Japanese property
subfiles.about: Urges a decision on Japanese property in Panama because it is deteriorating.
subfiles.summary: The embassy referred to its earlier despatches and telegrams concerning Japanese archives and property. It reported that the Panamanian Foreign Office had again inquired about disposition and warned that the property should be prepared and disposed of promptly.

subfiles.title: Instruction to Moscow concerning Soviet-held Japanese archives
subfiles.about: Clarifies that Moscow should seek reciprocal access to Japanese archives in Soviet custody.
subfiles.summary: The Department asked that the Soviet Foreign Office be kept informed of steps taken under MacArthur's directive. It called for a special effort to obtain access to information in Japanese archives held by the Soviet government on a reciprocal basis.

subfiles.title: Moscow inquiry about the applicability of archive circulars
subfiles.from: W. Averell Harriman, U.S. Embassy Moscow
subfiles.about: Asks whether the Department's circulars on Japanese archives require action in Moscow.
subfiles.summary: The embassy found it unclear whether the circulars were informational or operational. It noted that the British Embassy in Moscow also lacked instructions.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 27,307 on Japanese archives in Mexico
subfiles.from: Raymond H. Geist, U.S. Chargé d'Affaires ad interim, Mexico
subfiles.about: Reports stalled negotiations for delivery of Japanese archives to representatives of the four Allied powers.
subfiles.summary: Geist enclosed memoranda of Allied meetings held on November 5 and 7. He reported that the Swedish Chargé had not yet received a Mexican response and that the British ambassador had urged him to press the Foreign Office.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of conversation with the Swedish Chargé in Mexico
subfiles.about: Records discussions with Petersen about Swedish instructions to surrender Japanese property, funds, and archives.
subfiles.summary: Petersen said the property could be delivered to a representative designated by the United States, Britain, China, and the Soviet Union, possibly the Mexican government. The memorandum discusses notification of Mexican authorities, approximately 250,000 pesos and $24,000 in Japanese funds, and a four-drawer filing cabinet of unexamined archives.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of Allied meeting at the British Embassy in Mexico
subfiles.about: Records Allied discussion of Mexican consent and the procedure for receiving Japanese archives.
subfiles.summary: Representatives of Britain, China, the Soviet Union, and the United States agreed that the Swedish Chargé should notify the Mexican Foreign Office before transferring the archives. Although the Soviet representative initially pressed for immediate possession under MacArthur's instructions, all agreed to await Mexico's reply.

subfiles.title: San Salvador report on Japanese archives
subfiles.from: Gerhard Gade, U.S. Chargé d'Affaires ad interim, El Salvador
subfiles.about: Summarizes how Japanese archives in El Salvador were acquired and examined.
subfiles.summary: The Foreign Office took custody after the Spanish Chargé explained that delivery to a Swiss representative had been impossible when Spain severed relations with Japan. The archives were then delivered to the U.S. Embassy on behalf of the four powers and appeared to contain nothing of interest.

subfiles.title: Departmental distribution memorandum for San Salvador Despatch No. 553
subfiles.to: Military Intelligence Division; Office of Naval Intelligence; Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.about: Distributes the San Salvador report on Japanese archives to federal agencies.
subfiles.summary: The Department forwarded Despatch No. 553 for possible intelligence value. The enclosure was Gade's November 19 report entitled “Japanese Archives.”

subfiles.title: Costa Rica report of no Japanese records or property
subfiles.from: Raleigh C. Gibson, U.S. Embassy San José
subfiles.about: Reports that Costa Rica contained no Japanese diplomatic or consular records, archives, or property.
subfiles.summary: The embassy acknowledged the two November 16 circular telegrams. It stated categorically that no relevant Japanese records or property existed in Costa Rica.

subfiles.title: Departmental distribution memorandum for San José Despatch No. 1241
subfiles.to: Military Intelligence Division; Office of Naval Intelligence; Federal Bureau of Investigation; Office of Strategic Services
subfiles.about: Distributes Costa Rica's negative report on Japanese archives and property.
subfiles.summary: The Department forwarded Despatch No. 1241 to intelligence and investigative offices. The enclosure reported the absence of Japanese diplomatic or consular materials in Costa Rica.

subfiles.title: Quito despatch on Japanese archives and property in Ecuador
subfiles.from: George P. Shaw, U.S. Chargé d'Affaires ad interim, Ecuador
subfiles.about: Reports the examination of Japanese records in Ecuador and efforts to open a Japanese Legation safe.
subfiles.summary: A joint committee of legal, military, naval, and diplomatic officers found no material of interest in the correspondence already examined. Miscellaneous Japanese-language papers awaited translation, while the Ecuadorian Foreign Ministry employed a local expert to open the legation safe.

subfiles.title: Jidda report on the absence of Japanese representation
subfiles.from: William L. Sands, U.S. Chargé d'Affaires ad interim, Saudi Arabia
subfiles.about: Reports that neither Japan nor Germany had maintained diplomatic or consular representation in Saudi Arabia.
subfiles.summary: Sands answered the Department's circular concerning Japanese archives and property. He stated that no German or Japanese diplomatic or consular representation had ever existed in Saudi Arabia.

subfiles.title: Oslo telegram reporting no Japanese archives or property
subfiles.about: Repeats that no Japanese property, archives, or official records had been found in Norway.
subfiles.summary: The embassy referred to the Department's November 16 circulars. It repeated information previously sent in August that searches had produced no Japanese official materials.

subfiles.title: Ottawa information copy on Japanese archives and property in Canada
subfiles.about: Reports Canada's reluctance to take custody of Japanese archives and property.
subfiles.summary: Canadian officials would accept a Swiss transfer to U.S. representatives acting under Japanese instructions issued through MacArthur. The material comprised reportedly valueless archives in Ottawa and Vancouver and a Vancouver building that Canada wished to liquidate.

subfiles.title: Instruction to Rome regarding Japanese property at Vatican City
subfiles.about: Confirms that the October directive applied to Japanese representation at Vatican City.
subfiles.summary: The Department instructed Rome to allow a reasonable period for appropriate Japanese action. If action was not forthcoming, the embassy was to report again.

subfiles.title: Ottawa action copy on Japanese archives and property in Canada
subfiles.about: Duplicates the Ottawa report concerning Canadian reluctance to assume custody.
subfiles.summary: The action copy records Canada's willingness to let Swiss custodians deliver Japanese materials to U.S. representatives. It again identifies archives in Ottawa and Vancouver and a Vancouver building slated for liquidation.

subfiles.title: Vatican City telegram on missing Japanese instructions
subfiles.from: Harold H. Tittmann Jr., Vatican City
subfiles.about: Reports that the Japanese ambassador to the Vatican had not yet received instructions.
subfiles.summary: Montini told the U.S. representative that no instructions had arrived for the Japanese ambassador. The message followed an earlier Vatican report of November 8.

subfiles.title: Santiago telegram referring to completed reports
subfiles.from: Claude G. Bowers, U.S. Embassy Santiago
subfiles.about: States that earlier telegrams and despatches fully covered Chilean procedures and recommendations.
subfiles.summary: Bowers cited telegram 1401 and Despatches 13,036 and 13,047. Those communications described the examination of Japanese archives and the proposed disposition of property.

subfiles.title: Port-au-Prince request for clarification
subfiles.about: Questions whether the November 16 custody directive applied to Japanese consular archives in Haiti.
subfiles.summary: Wilson noted that neither Sweden nor Switzerland acted as protecting power in Haiti and that the embassy had already examined the archives. He suggested that the British representative would probably cooperate if instructed.

subfiles.title: Reply allowing Port-au-Prince to disregard the circular
subfiles.about: Tells the embassy that no further action under the November 16 circular is necessary.
subfiles.summary: The Department referred to the information already submitted from Haiti. On that basis it authorized the mission to disregard the circular mentioned in telegram 369.

subfiles.title: Ciudad Trujillo report on Japanese archives
subfiles.from: George F. Scherer, U.S. Chargé d'Affaires ad interim
subfiles.about: Refers the Department to an earlier report on surrender and examination of Japanese archives in Ciudad Trujillo.
subfiles.summary: Scherer answered the November 16 circular by citing Despatch No. 306 of September 4. That earlier despatch contained the substantive account of the archives' surrender and examination.

subfiles.title: Political Adviser's report on property of former Japanese officials in Germany and Austria
subfiles.about: Reports on property left by Japanese diplomatic personnel moved from Berlin to Bad Gastein.
subfiles.summary: The badly damaged text concerns goods and vehicles associated with Japanese officials, their families, and staff transferred from Berlin during the final phase of the war. It discusses military-government custody in the Salzburg area and references earlier reporting from the American Legation at Bern.

subfiles.title: Tirana report on Japanese archives and property
subfiles.about: Reports on the apparent absence of regular Japanese diplomatic property or archives in Albania.
subfiles.summary: The mission's response indicates that any Japanese presence was connected with the period of Italian occupation rather than a regular diplomatic or consular establishment. It therefore found no ordinary Japanese official property or archive to take over.

subfiles.title: Instruction on Japanese officials' property held in Austria
subfiles.about: Directs that property belonging to repatriated Japanese officials be retained in safe custody pending possible transfer to Switzerland.
subfiles.summary: Because the Japanese nationals had already sailed from Seattle for Japan, the Department canceled plans to ship their property to the United States. It asked military-government property control to hold the goods while Bern explored transfer to Swedish protection in Switzerland, and also requested notice when an automobile was returned by the Archbishop of Salzburg.

subfiles.title: Instruction to Tokyo repeating Dublin's complaint about the Japanese Consul General
subfiles.to: George Atcheson Jr., Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Asks Tokyo to compel the Japanese Consul General in Dublin to comply precisely with Allied transfer instructions.
subfiles.summary: Dublin reported that the consul general had returned an Allied memorandum with procedural objections and proposed alternative delivery arrangements. The Department recommended orders requiring his personal attendance, immediate compliance, and notification of the U.S. and British missions.

subfiles.title: Addis Ababa report of no Japanese property or archives
subfiles.from: Felix Cole, U.S. Legation Addis Ababa
subfiles.about: Repeats that no Japanese government property or archives were found in Ethiopia.
subfiles.summary: The legation stated that earlier reporting had already supplied the same information from the Ethiopian Foreign Office. Japanese personnel had left with the Italians before British East African forces captured Addis Ababa, so further information would have to be sought from the relevant command headquarters.

subfiles.title: Havana request for custody and storage authority
subfiles.from: R. Henry Norweb, U.S. Embassy Havana
subfiles.about: Seeks authority to accept Japanese property and archives and pay associated storage and removal expenses.
subfiles.summary: The Cuban Ministry of State was expected to ask that Japanese property be removed from its custody. Norweb requested authority for retroactive storage charges, movement to U.S. premises, and unilateral American custody if the British, Chinese, and Soviet representatives agreed.

subfiles.title: Tokyo notice that a Department circular had not been received
subfiles.about: Reports nonreceipt of the Department's October 25 circular concerning Japanese overseas records and property.
subfiles.summary: Atcheson learned of the communication through a Joint Chiefs of Staff message to CINCAFPAC. He informed the Department that the original circular itself had not reached the mission.

subfiles.title: Bogotá telegram on archives, funds, and sale of furniture
subfiles.about: Reports Allied plans for Japanese archives and funds and asks permission to sell Japanese furniture.
subfiles.summary: The British ambassador was to receive and store the archives, notify the Swiss Chargé about terminating legation rent, and discuss unfreezing Japanese funds with Colombia. British and Soviet representatives favored selling the furniture and asked whether the Allied committee could take custody of the funds.

subfiles.title: Internal comment on the proposed Bogotá policy response
subfiles.about: Comments on wording and the broader policy governing disposal of Japanese property.
subfiles.summary: The note records Clattenburg's proposed revision to the opening lines of the Bogotá reply. It suggests that the Department should adopt a consistent general policy for disposing of Japanese property.

subfiles.title: Unsent draft reply to Bogotá on furniture and funds
subfiles.about: Drafts rules for selling Japanese government furniture and controlling Japanese funds.
subfiles.summary: The draft authorizes sale of clearly government-owned furniture when storage is impracticable but prohibits sale of Japanese officials' private property. It approves Allied committee custody of funds, with accountable withdrawals for protection work, and asks Tokyo to clarify ownership of the Bogotá furniture.

subfiles.title: Instruction to The Hague on direct Dutch custody
subfiles.about: Transmits Japan's request that the Netherlands take direct custody of Japanese records and property.
subfiles.summary: General MacArthur reported that Japan had no protecting power in the Netherlands or Netherlands East Indies. The embassy was instructed to convey the request for direct Dutch action to the Foreign Office.

subfiles.title: Luxembourg despatch on Japanese archives
subfiles.from: George Platt Waller, U.S. Chargé d'Affaires ad interim, Luxembourg
subfiles.about: Describes Japanese archives sealed and retained by the Luxembourg government.
subfiles.summary: Former honorary consul J. P. Arendt surrendered commercial and consular dossiers, reports, stamps, and a shield to the Foreign Office. Waller expected Luxembourg to retain sovereign custody as an Allied state but said U.S. access for further inspection would be available.

subfiles.title: Memorandum to the State-War-Navy Coordinating Committee on Dutch custody
subfiles.about: Explains the State Department's response to MacArthur's report concerning Japanese property in Dutch territory.
subfiles.summary: The Department had already asked The Hague to act on Japan's request for direct Dutch custody in the Netherlands and Netherlands East Indies. Because MacArthur's directive expressly permitted that arrangement, Hickerson concluded that no further action was needed.

subfiles.title: Wellington despatch on German and Japanese archives and property
subfiles.from: Prescott Childs, U.S. Chargé d'Affaires ad interim, New Zealand
subfiles.about: Describes New Zealand's handling of German records and its plans to treat Japanese property in the same manner.
subfiles.summary: German furniture had been auctioned and sealed archive cases stored in Parliament Buildings, while no detailed examination had yet occurred. Japanese property and archives were to pass from the Swiss consul to the Ministry of External Affairs, which offered U.S. examiners access.

subfiles.title: Departmental distribution memorandum for Wellington Despatch No. 1072
subfiles.to: Military Intelligence Division; Office of Naval Intelligence; Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.about: Distributes the New Zealand report on German and Japanese archives and property.
subfiles.summary: The Department circulated Prescott Childs's November 29 despatch to federal agencies. The enclosure described archive custody and property disposal in New Zealand.

subfiles.title: Budapest telegram referring to an earlier archives report
subfiles.from: H. F. Arthur Schoenfeld, U.S. Mission Budapest
subfiles.about: States that the Japanese archives and property question had already been covered in an earlier airgram.
subfiles.summary: The mission answered the November 16 circular by citing Airgram No. 715 of September 29. No new substantive information was supplied in the telegram.

subfiles.title: Tokyo report of orders sent to the Japanese Consul General in Dublin
subfiles.about: Reports that the Japanese government was directed to issue urgent instructions to its consul general in Dublin.
subfiles.summary: The Supreme Commander acted on November 26 in response to the Department's November 22 message. The directions followed the compliance measures recommended by the Allied representatives in Dublin.

subfiles.title: Cairo airgram on Egypt's claim to custody of Japanese archives
subfiles.from: C. B. Lyon, U.S. Legation Cairo
subfiles.about: Reports Egypt's decision to retain Japanese archives and property while allowing Allied access.
subfiles.summary: The Egyptian Foreign Ministry argued that, as an Allied belligerent and territorial state, Egypt should preserve the records and goods, following its precedent for German property. Britain considered the arrangement reasonable, the Soviet representative sought instructions, China would follow the American position, and the Swiss minister asked Bern how to respond.

subfiles.title: Handwritten Japanese Affairs recommendation on the Moscow archives question
subfiles.about: Recommends delaying action on the proposed approach to Moscow.
subfiles.summary: The damaged handwritten note invokes Harriman's recommendations and doubts that pressing the question would produce useful results. It favors suspending action until further evidence or instructions are available.

subfiles.title: Special Projects memorandum on Moscow Telegram No. 4030
subfiles.about: Refers the political questions raised by Moscow's objections to seeking Japanese archives.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum notes that examination of Japanese archives formed part of the Department's general program. Because the embassy's concerns were essentially political, Special Projects sought the views of the relevant regional and Japanese-affairs offices.

subfiles.title: Handwritten disposition note on answering Moscow
subfiles.about: Recommends maintaining the status quo rather than instructing Moscow to approach the Soviet government.
subfiles.summary: The note records Chapin's view that a reply was unnecessary and that inaction was preferable to placing the embassy on record as retreating from earlier instructions. It requests preparation of a telegram only if the reviewing office disagrees.

subfiles.title: Moscow Telegram No. 4030 opposing an immediate archives approach
subfiles.from: W. Averell Harriman, U.S. Embassy Moscow
subfiles.about: Explains why the embassy opposed seeking reciprocal access to Japanese archives in Soviet custody.
subfiles.summary: Harriman believed valuable Japanese records had probably been destroyed or would be withheld and that reciprocity might require sharing more useful Allied-held material. He also warned that an approach could disrupt negotiations over Soviet participation in control of Japan and noted British opposition to raising the issue.

subfiles.title: Rome telegram on Swedish noncustody of Japanese property in Italy
subfiles.about: Reports Sweden's position that the United States could take over Japanese property in Italy.
subfiles.summary: The Swedish Legation said Stockholm had requested surrender of Japanese property only where Sweden had actually assumed protective custody. Because the Rome legation had never taken over such property, it raised no objection to U.S. custody; Soviet and Chinese comments were being sought.

subfiles.title: Helsinki airgram on unopened Japanese safes and archives
subfiles.from: Benjamin M. Hulley, U.S. Legation Helsinki
subfiles.about: Reports that a full Finnish inventory awaited the opening of Japanese safes and filing cabinets.
subfiles.summary: Hulley referred to an earlier telegram for all presently available information. He recommended appointment of an expert by the three custodial governments to inventory and study the archives and noted that instructions about German property had not arrived.

subfiles.title: Instruction to Helsinki on storage, sale, and trust funds
subfiles.about: Sets policy for Japanese official property and funds held in Finland.
subfiles.summary: Official property was generally to be stored, though government-owned items could be sold when storage was impracticable; private property was not to be sold. All mission, personal, and sale-derived funds were to enter a jointly controlled Allied trust account, with limited accountable withdrawals for custody and relief expenses.

subfiles.title: Lima Despatch No. 667 on transfer of Japanese property and funds
subfiles.from: Edward E. Trueblood, U.S. Chargé d'Affaires ad interim, Peru
subfiles.about: Gives a detailed account of the Allied takeover of Japanese archives, furniture, safes, and funds in Peru.
subfiles.summary: American, British, and Chinese representatives moved furniture to the U.S. ambassador's residence, placed safes and boxes under U.S. control, and deposited $143,641.55 under three-power seals at the Royal Bank of Canada. The Swedish Legation retained about 250,000 soles for Japanese protection work, while safe-opening, archive examination, storage conditions, and accumulated expenses remained unresolved.

subfiles.title: Swedish notification of the transfer in Peru
subfiles.from: Lennart Petri, Swedish Legation in Lima
subfiles.about: Notifies Peru that Japanese consular and diplomatic property and archives are being handed to the American, British, and Chinese embassies.
subfiles.summary: Petri stated that the transfer followed urgent instructions from Sweden and a request by the Japanese government. He also advised that the Swedish Legation had been asked to continue protecting Japanese subjects in Peru.

subfiles.title: U.S. note to Peru confirming transfer and cash receipt
subfiles.to: Javier Correa Elías, Peruvian Minister of Foreign Affairs
subfiles.about: Formally informs Peru of the Allied transfer of Japanese property, archives, and dollar currency.
subfiles.summary: Trueblood wrote in agreement with the Chinese and British representatives. The note specifically recorded receipt of $143,641.55 purported to be in U.S. dollars, in addition to physical property and archives.

subfiles.title: Joint receipt for Japanese official property and cash in Peru
subfiles.from: Lennart Petri; C. J. Pao; Walter St. Clair Roberts; Edward E. Trueblood
subfiles.to: Swedish, Chinese, British, and American diplomatic missions in Lima
subfiles.about: Certifies the handover and receipt of Japanese official property and $143,641.55 in cash.
subfiles.summary: The receipt covers the attached furniture and archive inventory and the dollar fund. It leaves some furniture available for continuing Swedish protection work and states that Peruvian soles remained with the Swedish Chargé pending intergovernmental agreement.

subfiles.title: Inventory of furnishings of the Japanese Legation in Peru, List No. 1
subfiles.from: Custodians of Japanese Legation property in Peru
subfiles.about: Begins an itemized Spanish-language inventory of furniture from the Japanese minister's residence in Peru.
subfiles.summary: The opening page lists beds, mattresses, mirrored dressing tables, wardrobes, dining furniture, tables, pianos, Philips and Victor radios, lamps, screens, pictures, and bronze planters. The numbered inventory continues beyond this section.
